title: Viral Video Shows IndiGo Passengers Standing in Aisle, Sharing Food Mid-Flight
excerpt: Footage from a Delhi-bound IndiGo flight shows passengers standing in the aisle and passing food around despite crew warnings — the latest in a string of viral cabin-etiquette incidents.
body:
• A video circulating on social media, reported by NDTV, India Today, News18 and Asianet Newsable, shows passengers on a Delhi-bound IndiGo flight standing in the aisle and passing food to fellow travellers despite the cabin crew's repeated warnings to sit down.
  • Commenters dubbed the scene a "local train," and the clip has reignited debate over cabin safety rules and passenger etiquette on Indian domestic flights.
  • Standing passengers are a genuine safety hazard: anyone unseated during unexpected turbulence risks serious injury, and blocked aisles slow emergency evacuations.
  • You can carry home food on Indian domestic flights, but crew instructions are binding — when asked to sit, sit. If turbulence hits while you are standing in the aisle, nothing is holding you down.

The video

In the latest viral cabin clip to grip Indian social media, passengers on a Delhi-bound IndiGo flight are seen standing in the aisle and handing food to one another as the aircraft is airborne. According to reports from NDTV, India Today, News18 and Asianet Newsable, the passengers kept moving about and distributing food even as the cabin crew repeatedly asked them to return to their seats. The sight of a queue of flyers trading plates mid-flight drew the inevitable comparison — "local train" — and the video has since driven a fresh round of argument online about how people behave in the air.

A recurring pattern

This is not an isolated embarrassment for Indian aviation. In August 2026, a video showed a family of around 15 passengers on an IndiGo flight unpacking boxes of theplas, dhoklas and other homemade food and passing plates around while the plane was in motion — an episode that split social media between those calling it harmless fun and those calling it a civic-sense failure.

The pattern goes back further. In January 2024, passengers on a Goa-Delhi IndiGo flight that was diverted to Mumbai were filmed sitting on the tarmac eating their meals; the aviation security regulator BCAS fined IndiGo ₹1.2 crore and Mumbai airport's operator ₹60 lakh, with the DGCA adding a ₹30 lakh penalty on the airport for the safety violations. Just last month, a video surfaced of passengers standing in the aisle of an Air India Express flight while the aircraft was moving on the runway, prompting the Union Civil Aviation Minister to stress that there should be no compromise on security in airport operations.

Why crew warnings are not optional

Etiquette is only half the story. Aviation safety rules require passengers to be seated with seatbelts fastened during critical phases of flight and whenever the seatbelt sign is on — and crew instructions carry the force of law. An unseated passenger in unexpected turbulence becomes a projectile; blocked aisles turn a routine evacuation into a dangerous one. India has seen that regulators treat viral misbehaviour as a compliance event, not a joke — the ₹1.2 crore BCAS fine in 2024 is the precedent.

The etiquette debate

Online, reactions split along familiar lines. Some viewers defended the passengers as a group simply sharing a meal, pointing out that carrying home food on board is allowed on domestic carriers and that the group cleaned up after itself. Others were less forgiving: a packed aircraft cabin is a confined shared space for several hours, food smells linger for the entire journey, and moving around with plates disturbs passengers who never signed up for the picnic. The sharpest criticism landed on the crew's warnings being ignored — whatever one's view of mid-air snacks, defying the people responsible for everyone's safety is where sympathy runs out.

What's next

So far there has been no public statement from IndiGo on this incident. What bears watching is whether the DGCA or BCAS treats this like the 2024 tarmac episode — an incident serious enough to warrant show-cause notices and fines — or lets it pass as a social-media talking point. Either way, the message for flyers is the one the crew was already delivering: stay seated.
